title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Do absolute constants \(C,d>0\) and a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol exist that, for every n and every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations, use at most \(Cn^{d}\) queries to produce a complete exactly envy-free allocation, allowing disconnected pieces?
definitions: The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent i has an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure \(\mu _{i}\): values are nonnegative, countably additive, \(\mu _{i}([0,1])=1\) and \(\mu _{i}(\{x\})=0\) for every point x. No density formula, bounded-density promise or random valuation model is supplied. The protocol learns valuations only through exact queries: \(Eval(i,x,y)\) returns \(\mu _{i}([x,y]); Cut(i,x,\alpha )\), with \(0\le \alpha \le \mu _{i}([x,1])\), returns a point \(y\ge x\) for which \(\mu _{i}([x,y])=\alpha\). Endpoints used by the protocol are 0, 1 and previously returned cut marks; interval values can be combined by additivity. If several cut points satisfy a query, the protocol must remain correct for any valid response. Count each evaluation or cut query as one; finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-complexity bound. Output a partition \((A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n})\) of the entire cake into finite unions of intervals with endpoints among the known marks. Assign cut endpoints arbitrarily, since every agent values them at zero. Require \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for every ordered pair i,j. There is no unallocated residue, approximation error, randomization, or connected-piece requirement. The bound \(Cn^{d}\) is uniform over all valuation profiles and valid query responses.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic protocol with the stated worst-case polynomial query bound, or prove that every such protocol has superpolynomial worst-case query complexity as n grows. A lower bound on the number of queries used by one known protocol is not a general impossibility result. A finite bound depending arbitrarily on n, an average-case polynomial bound, or a polynomial protocol permitting positive envy or discarded cake leaves this question open.
why: A central information-complexity question in fair division: how many exact preference queries are necessary to allocate an entire divisible resource without envy?

importance.reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.

progress.text: Brams–Taylor give an always-terminating protocol for arbitrary n, without a bound depending only on n.
Procaccia proves an \(\Omega (n^{2})\) query lower bound for envy-free cake cutting.
Aziz–Mackenzie give a bounded deterministic protocol; the full manuscript’s latest revision is August 2017.
Brânzei–Nisan study query complexity for approximate fairness and explain the distinction between connected and fragmented exact allocations.
Sokolov posts an improved \(n^{8n^{2}(1+o(1))}\) query upper bound.
Chèze’s article is published online, giving a polynomial query bound with high probability over its random valuation model; journal volume 67 appears in 2026.
Ye–Bai post a deterministic \(n^{O(1)}2^{n}\)-query protocol for complete exact envy-free allocation. This reported preprint bound remains exponential.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Polynomial worst-case query complexity remains open. The latest checked general upper bound is the \(n^{O(1)}2^{n}\) protocol reported in the Ye–Bai preprint of 4 September 2026; Chèze’s polynomial result is over random valuation profiles.

context_blocks.text: Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely \(1/n\). The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is \(\Omega (n^{2})\) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the \(\Theta (n \log  n)\) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to \(n^{8n^{2}(1+o(1))}\). That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to \(2^{(8+o(1))n^{2} \log _{2}n}\), although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited \(2025/2026\) average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using \(n^{O(1)}2^{n}\) queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. A helper construction uses exhaustive search after the relevant values have been elicited; Appendix C explains its deterministic choices and implementation through ordinary Robertson–Webb queries. Expensive transcript processing is allowed in the present question. Thus the reported single-exponential query bound should not be advertised as an equally fast bit-time algorithm, and it still does not give polynomially many queries.

Chèze’s inherited article studies a probability distribution on valuation profiles, following a full-independence framework. Under its uniform model, the probability of needing at least \(n^{12}\) queries tends to zero. This probability concerns the sampled preferences, rather than random bits used by a protocol facing an arbitrary fixed profile. Rare or specially chosen valuations remain relevant to the worst-case question. The article appeared online in September 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume.

Approximate envy-freeness creates another distinct regime. Bounds polynomial in n and inverse tolerance can produce small positive envy, including versions with connected pieces. Sending the tolerance to zero does not yield a finite exact protocol if the query count diverges. Exactness, completeness, access through queries and unrestricted disconnected allocations are therefore all part of this card’s answer criterion.

The fundamental issue is the amount of preference information needed for an exact global fairness guarantee. A polynomial protocol would show that the enormous historical bounds reflect limitations of the constructions rather than an intrinsic elicitation barrier. A superpolynomial lower bound would reveal a sharp information cost of exact envy-freeness even when computational work between queries is unrestricted.

sentences: Envy-free cake cutting divides a continuous resource so that nobody prefers another person's share under their own valuation.
The reviewed question asks for an exact complete allocation using polynomially many deterministic Robertson–Webb queries.
Disconnected pieces are allowed, and local computation between queries is unrestricted.
A polynomial protocol would identify a manageable amount of preference information sufficient for exact global fairness.
The saved review records a recent single-exponential query upper-bound preprint but distinguishes it from polynomial complexity, approximate fairness, and favorable average-case valuation models.
